storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere nearby tonight. Strong high pressure is keeping skies clear and the air calm, so the cove is no different from the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer: the Sound (64°F) is already warmer than the air (55°F) at 4 PM, and the gap only widens as the air cools to about 51°F by 8 PM.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: A strong high-pressure system (around 1034 mb) sits over southern New England. KOKX radar shows no echoes to track, there are no NWS watches, warnings or advisories, and the model shows zero instability (CAPE 0 J/kg) with weak wind shear of about 13 kt. Nothing is set up to produce thunderstorms.

Local modifier: On summer afternoons, cool Sound water under warmer air forms a stable marine layer that often weakens storms before they reach the cove. Tonight it works the other way. The Sound is at 63.7°F and the air is 55°F, so the water is about 8°F warmer than the air. No protective layer can form.

Through the evening: The Sound holds its temperature while the air cools after sunset (6:08 PM). The air is forecast to reach about 51°F by 8 PM, which pushes the water about 13°F above the air. That doesn't affect storm risk tonight because there is nothing to buffer. Warm water under cold air is the classic autumn setup for lake-effect-style showers and gusty marine conditions, but tonight the air is too dry and the high too strong for either.

Most likely outcome: A dry, clear, cooling evening across the whole area, with the cove behaving just like inland Westchester and Fairfield County.

What would change the call: Nothing in the current data points to a change before midnight. A shift would need a fast-moving system from the west, and both radar and the model show none.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, near calm
wind.tactics_blurb: Not enough wind to race: 1–2 kt all evening, and the direction swings from southwest to east after sunset. If you do go out, stay in the middle of the course and sail toward any dark patch of ripples you can see.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Regime call: Tonight has a light gradient wind with no sea breeze. A sea breeze needs land and air warmer than the water. The Sound is at 63.7°F, about 8°F warmer than the 55°F air (an air–water temperature difference of −8.3°F), so no thermal can develop. Only 26% of coastal stations show a southerly, and the strong high overhead (about 1034 mb) leaves almost no pressure gradient to drive any background wind.

What's on the water now: At 4 PM the Riverside YC anemometer reads S at 4 kt, averaging 2.4 kt over 10 minutes. The waterfront stations in Old Greenwich and Port Chester read under 2 kt in every direction. The HRRR model has the cove at 1–2 kt through 8 PM.

Shift character: The faint southwesterly fades toward calm around sunset (6:08 PM). After that the model backs the drift to the southeast and then the east at about 2 kt. With this little wind, direction means little. Expect it to wander through large arcs from one minute to the next, with no pattern to play. This is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day, so the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply. The model (SSE) and the current observations (SSW) also disagree by more than 50°, so direction confidence is low.

Where the pressure is: There is no organized breeze to favor either side of the course. With the water warmer than the air, any faint drainage flow off the land after dark would come from the north. That is not a reliable source of pressure. Stay in the middle of the course and go wherever you can see ripples.

What racers will feel: Mostly drifting, with 2–4 kt at best. Most fleets would not start in this, and any race already under way is likely to be shortened or abandoned. It will also be chilly on the water, with air in the low 50s after sunset.
